Mallory crawler · operations

Daily health check

One command that exercises the running crawler end to end and reports, per subsystem, whether it is healthy — so when something breaks, the red line tells you where, before you open a single log.

63checks
6subsystems
1×per day, on the DC
0writes to production

Why it exists

The crawler is a stack of moving parts — four fetch tiers, twelve crawl instances, an ingest store, two dashboards, a control plane. When someone says "the dashboard is empty" or "nothing's crawling," the first and most expensive question is always where.

This suite answers that up front. Every check is small, runs against the live system, and its one-line result names the exact thing it verified. A daily run is a labelled map of the whole stack: green everywhere means healthy; a single red line points straight at the fault instead of sending you into the logs to find it.

It is not the unit-test suite (crawler/tests, orchestrator/tests). Those prove the code is correct in isolation. This proves the deployed system is doing its job right now — the two are complementary, and the logic area can fold the unit suites in.

The four tiers it verifies

Each page is fetched by the cheapest tier that can serve it; the crawler escalates only when a tier is refused, because each rung costs roughly 50× the one below. The suite proves every rung both works (an active canary fetch) and is being used (pages served by it recently).

C1
Live fetchhttpx + curl_cffi Chrome TLS/JA3

The cheap default: no browser, fast, most pages. If this stops serving, throughput collapses.

baseline cost
C2
WaybackInternet Archive replay

Used when the origin is dead, blocked, or gone (404/410) — recover the page from the archive.

~50× C1
C3
CamoFoxCamoufox stealth browser (Firefox pool)

For everything the origin refuses otherwise: JS-only pages, bot walls, captchas.

~50× C2
C4
Host solverbrowser on a real-GPU workstation, via reverse tunnel

The one thing C3 can't clear: an interactive Cloudflare / Incapsula wall. The last rung; opt-in.

~50× C3

What it checks

Sixty-three checks across six areas. Each area answers one operational question; the sample check names below are the actual ones that print in the report.

services

10 checks

Is every moving part up and reachable? The critical liveness floor — if these fail, the rest is noise.

  • ingest_health · orchestrator_health · crawler_api_health
  • postgres_reachable · documents_table
  • minio_raw_bucket · camofox_reachable
  • 3 more (stats, metrics, same-DB check)

tiers

8 checks

Do C1–C4 actually fetch, and are they serving pages? Active canary probe + passive "served recently" per tier.

  • c1_active_httpx · c1_passive_recent
  • c2_active_wayback · c2_passive_recent
  • c3_active_camofox · c3_passive_recent
  • c4_active_solver · c4_passive_recent

coverage

10 checks

Are sites being crawled properly? Catches the classic failure classes, not just "is it running".

  • freshness: recent ingest
  • beyond-seed: depth accumulates
  • one-page sites · zero-page enrolled sources
  • text capture (not empty shells) · gate sanity
  • 4 more (volume, html, distribution, pdfs)

delta

6 checks

Does the store's accounting reconcile and is push/verify trustworthy? The numbers on the dashboards must add up.

  • reconciliation: sum(pages) == documents
  • verify: local delta coherent
  • verify: no delivered-but-missing
  • push/status · centre/check · orch vs ingest

dashboards

20 checks

Does every dashboard-backing endpoint serve real, self-consistent data within a sane time — including the slow ones that used to time out?

  • ingest: summary / sources / types / quality / recent / search
  • orch: data/summary / data/sources?limit=5000 / logs/sites
  • crawler-api: metrics / batch status / dashboard
  • consistency: totals reconcile across dashboards

logic

9 checks

Is the control plane behaving? Maintenance, categories, scheduler, fleet, sharding, the daily lane.

  • maintenance flag is off
  • category buckets incl general
  • fleet instances all reporting · shard distribution
  • scheduler alive · daily lane self-consistent
  • 2 guarded unit-suite runners (opt-in)

How it runs

Once a day, on the data-centre box, as a read-only overlay on the live stack. It shares the stack's network and .env, so it reaches the real services and the real corpus.

1
A timer fires

A systemd timer (or cron) runs the wrapper once a day and keeps a timestamped log.

2
A one-shot container runs the suite

The crawler image already has the deps + network; the healthcheck/ package is mounted in, so editing a check needs no rebuild.

3
63 checks run, grouped by area

Each records its own result and timing. Read-only throughout — the only outbound traffic is a few tier canary fetches.

4
A verdict + exit code

HEALTHY / UNHEALTHY, a per-area report, and a JSON copy for trending. A non-zero exit is what a timer or cron alerts on.

# run it once, by hand
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.healthcheck.yml run --rm healthcheck

# or the daily wrapper (logging + pruning + exit code)
./healthcheck/run_daily.sh

# one area while debugging
python -m healthcheck.run tiers coverage

Two safety rules, built in

A health check that harms the thing it measures is worse than none. Two hazards are designed out at the framework level.

Never detoast the corpus

The DB helper refuses any query that selects main_text/html — decompressing those TOAST columns over the whole corpus is a known outage. Checks use text_len/html_len instead.

Read-only against production

No writes, no crawl dispatch, no restarts. The suite observes; it never changes state. Even the push/verify checks only read the delta — they never press Push.

Unit suites are opt-in

The unit tests share the production DB, so they are not run by default — only with an explicit flag and a separate, non-production test database.

Bounded and cheap

Every call has a timeout; the whole run is light enough for a busy box. A slow endpoint is reported (with its seconds) rather than allowed to hang.

How to read a run

The report is the whole point: scannable, grouped, and specific. Each line is status · name · time · what it observed. PASS is healthy, SKIP means a feature is off or a dependency isn't wired here (not a failure), FAIL is the thing to look at.

  mallory-healthcheck — daily
[tiers]
  PASS c1_active_httpx        0.4s  example.com 200, 1.2KB via httpx/impersonate
  PASS c1_passive_recent      0.1s  18,432 docs via c1_live in last 48h
  PASS c3_active_camofox      1.1s  2/2 CamoFox pool servers healthy
  SKIP c4_active_solver       0.0s  C4 disabled: CRAWLER_HOST_SOLVER_URL unset

[coverage]
  PASS freshness: recent ingest   0.3s  4,901 docs in last 48h
  FAIL one-page sites             0.6s  71% of crawled sources hold 1 page
  PASS text capture               0.4s  96% of recent docs have text

[delta]
  PASS reconciliation             0.5s  sum(pages)=2,131,004 == documents
================================================================
UNHEALTHY: 61 passed, 1 failed, 1 skipped in 41.2s

One red line, and you already know: crawling is alive and text is landing, but too many sites stopped at their seed page — a coverage problem to chase, not a dead crawler. That is the difference between a five-minute fix and an afternoon in the logs.

Where it lives

healthcheck/ in the crawler repo — framework (hc.py, run.py), the six checks/ modules, the compose overlay, and the systemd units under deploy/.

Built area-by-area so each subsystem's checks are grounded in its real endpoints and columns. Extend it by dropping one function into the matching checks/<area>.py.
